title: Vangisa the poet
hookLine: the poet-monk who praised the Buddha in verse on the spot (Theragatha, Vangisa)

cards: It occurs to me, Blessed One. It occurs to me, Fortunate One. In a sutta of the Samyutta, a monk stands up in the middle of a teaching, puts his robe over one shoulder, raises his joined hands and says it, twice.
Something is coming, and he can't sit on it. The Buddha answers: then let it come to you, Vangisa. And Vangisa speaks a poem of praise, right there, to the whole gathering.

teach.h: DRUNK ON POETRY, VILLAGE TO VILLAGE.
teach.b: First, who he was before. In his verses in the Theragatha, Vangisa looks back: once, drunk on poetry, I wandered from village to village, town to town. Then I saw the Buddha, gone beyond all things, and faith arose in me.
He didn't stop being a poet when he became a monk. The poetry turned toward something. Second, the danger in the gift.
Another sutta in the same collection says that Vangisa, because of his quickness with words, looked down on other monks, good and steady ones.

Then he caught himself and turned his poetry on his own pride: drop the conceit, he tells himself, it leads nowhere good. The same tongue that praised could also sneer, and he knew it. Third, the question.
After one of his poems of praise, the Buddha asks what a writing teacher might ask: Vangisa, were these verses thought out beforehand, or did they come to you on the spot? On the spot, he says.
Then, says the Buddha, let a few more come. He doesn't warn him off spontaneity. He asks for more.
Fourth, what the praise is for. Vangisa's poems praise the Buddha, Sariputta, the teaching, the gathered monks. Praise, in these suttas, isn't flattery or a performance for the poet.
It's seeing clearly what's good in front of you and saying so, out loud, while the person can hear it.
For a man who once used words to look down on people, that's a turn worth singing about.

how: Vangisa's poems are kept in the Theragatha and in a chapter of the Samyutta named for him, and verses of praise to the Buddha, the teaching and the community are chanted in Buddhist communities to this day.

o: it occurs to me; something comes to mind
let me recite what I learned by heart
I humbly ask permission to speak

games.q: Vangisa the poet: tap the pairs.

s: Vangisa worked out his poems of praise ahead of time
asked by the Buddha, he says they came to him on the spot.
Vangisa's gift with words once made him look down on others
a sutta says he looked down on good monks, then turned his poetry on his own conceit.
the Buddha told Vangisa to stop making poems
the Buddha asked him for a few more verses.

games.q: you're Vangisa. in the middle of a teaching, a poem rises in you. what do you do?
o: stay quiet: it's not your turn to speak.
stand, ask permission, and speak it.
games.why: he stands, robe on one shoulder, hands joined, and says it occurs to me. the Buddha tells him to let it come, and he speaks it to the gathering.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose goodness you've seen up close and maybe never named, and let a single line about them form; it doesn't need to rhyme or be clever, only true, like she stays when things get hard.
Turn the line over once or twice until it sounds right, then rest with it, and with the person it's about.

wordCard.voice: Patibhati. It occurs to me: what Vangisa the poet said when a verse arrived, a monk who learned to use his gift to praise what's good, on the spot. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali patibhati: it occurs to me, it comes to me. Vangisa's words when a poem arrives.

carryVoice: Your line: praise, in verse. Praise that sees clearly is a gift, not flattery. Day eight hundred ten, done.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 8.3 (looking down on well-behaved monks) and 8.8 (planned or spontaneous)
